title: For developer: missing a lot, please read everything
body:
Correct me if Im misunderstanding anything. This is coming from a developer of multiple years

first of all let’s start off with how almost every single feature is paid. I know that the you developers need the payment to continue working on it well, but some features that are behind a paywall are GENUINELY necessities that shouldn’t cost a dollar. For example you can’t even intervention block more than a single app without getting the subscription, and if you tested the app well you would know that most people need to block more than 1 app. Surprise surprise if TikTok is blocked I’ll just switch to Insta.

second I shouldn’t have to create a shortcuts automation every time I add an app to one sec. other focus apps allow you to block multiple apps in seconds. “linking” an app twice for each block/intervention is a bit redundant, it should just let me choose what apps i wanna block from a list. 

then there’s the fact there’s very little securing of your blocks unless you pay. it’s TOO easy to just delete the Shortcuts Automation to stop the app blocking forever, or just use the TikTok.com instead of the TikTok app (cause strict blocking is paid too…)

It’s also REALLY annoying how a bug fix was turned into a Pro feature (Intentional App Switching). Normally if you got timed out from an app, you would close the app for 5 minutes, take a break, and come back after 5 minutes. Well with one sec you have to wait the full 5 minutes INSIDE the app to be able to use it again, or you’ll have to wait for the timeout to expire every, single time you reopen the app. Only way to fix this? get pro which is stupid 

The last straw was when the stupid intervention feature wasn’t working properly at all. I needed to use YouTube for an emergency but every time I went through the intervention YouTube was still blocked. Don’t make so many features paid if the basic ones aren’t even working properly.

Developer, correct me if I misunderstood anything but in my opinion it’s not the most effective and a bit cash grabby. there are other focus apps like Opal with the same features for free

title: Changed my life! Would recommend one big change though
body:
I LOVE one sec! I've been using it for at least a couple of years now. The combination of using One Sec and deleting the instagram app has basically changed my life. The best features are: 
1. Being able to set time frame blocks for certain apps and websites (so helpful for not scrolling during work hours or late at night!)
2. Being able to set a timer for how many minutes you'd like to spend in the app before another intervention
3. Just making my distracting apps and websites less of a favorable activity (aka more annoying bc I keep getting interrupted!)

I would only make one big change to improve this app. Let's use Facebook for example. When you click on Facebook, it immediately runs OneSec and starts an animation such as the screen going dark for several seconds. This is designed to slow you down and help you consider clearly whether you actually want to be opening that app right now. It's meant to prevent mindlessly opening up apps. When the animation is finished,  it asks you if you really want to open facebook. Well, you've already waited the several seconds for the animation- you may as well open it! You open facebook. 

If onesec asked me if I wanted to open it BEFORE the intervention animation started, that would be a game changer. That way it would be a trade: you have to pay to open this app- you can only open it if you wait several boring seconds first. Then if you click yes to continue to the intervention, and then the intervention finishes, it still asks you what your reason for opening the app is and how many minutes you want to spend on there before another intervention. 

Mane this could be a setting you ca toggle on and off, so if anyone doesn't like that system they can opt out. THEN the app would be perfect. What do we think?

title: Strong blocking, but missing real accountability
body:
This app does a good job enforcing Screen Time limits, but it falls short as an accountability tool.

Like most Screen Time apps, it relies on three mechanisms:
	•	app time limits
	•	unlocks / temporary access
	•	scheduled blocks

The problem is that following or breaking these rules isn’t meaningfully tracked. Users can:
	•	repeatedly use unlocks
	•	change limits or schedules after enforcement starts
	•	revoke Screen Time permissions and re-enable later

…without any persistent history or consequence inside the app. That makes it easy to undermine your own rules quietly, which defeats the purpose for serious users.

What would make this a 5-star app:
	•	an accountability history (unlock usage, schedule adherence, rule changes)
	•	logging Screen Time permission revocations/restores
	•	an integrity metric (did I keep my word or not)
	•	brief, optional reflection prompts at key moments (before unlocks, after rule changes)
	•	weekly summaries focused on accountability, not just usage minutes
	•	a place to define and revisit why you’re limiting apps, so behavior change is internal, not just enforced

Blocking alone changes behavior temporarily.
Accountability, integrity tracking, and reflection change it long-term.

If these additions were made, this would easily be a 5-star app.

title: Great app, but…
body: This is a very clever application that does precisely what it’s advertised to. It requires a form of intervention before opening an app of your choice, and this is highly customizable. There are lots of interventions to choose from, and how long you want them to be. You can also have it choose a random exercise for you, and it supports website blocking as well, which is nice. You can also set up a bedtime schedule where it blocks all apps and websites. It provides an informative dashboard detailing approximately how much time you saved. However, I really can’t get behind the modern era of subscription based apps. Especially for the lifetime license costing a whopping FIFTY dollars, and SEVENTY for a “family plan”. I don’t have any problem supporting independent developers and paying for software, but I personally feel like this is overpriced for what it does. Most of it is just relying on the iOS shortcuts functionality anyway, and all the app is doing is showing a pretty GUI and recording the time. You could replicate something similar in shortcuts (although not entirely, like website blocking for instance.) If you don’t mind the cost, go for it, but I would probably pay $15 maximum for a lifetime license, not $50. Especially considering many people using this are likely college students.

author: Brin Ann

title: A great app that shows great promise
body:
I’m a student who has been struggling with procrastination for as long as I can remember. My phone, through social media and video games, has often been my source of that. I’ve tried other screen time apps in a desperate attempt to fix my problem, but all of them are easy to bypass and default back to wasting time. I was afraid that I would never be able to break the cycle. 

One Sec is the only program that forces you to reflect. And I mean, really, it forces you to reflect on yourself before you open the app that you designed. There’s nothing fancy about it - no bells and whistles like the other apps. That’s because change doesn’t come with bells and whistles, it comes from within. I’ve been using One Sec for only a day and I’ve managed to drop my average screen time about an hour and a half. It’s incredible, and I’m really giddy about how much I’ve been able to improve myself in only a day.

That being said, the downside of One Sec is that it doesn’t have any bells and whistles. You have to manually implement the shortcuts for all of the apps you want to block, and that is the meat and potatoes of this app - you don’t get much else that significantly helps you stop overusing apps. On top of that, the dashboard (overview) page of the app has very little content besides the list of apps that you blocked by hand and how much time you’ve saved through using One Sec (which seems inaccurate as I tend to spend a lot more time than three minutes every time I clicked on an app). 

But overall, this app is a great program that can help you beat overuse. More content and programs are sure to come as this app is just beginning, and I really look forward to it. I think that there are a lot of great things that can happen with this app, such as more content being added to the overview page (overall screen time, usage trend graphs, times you’ve continued to use the app despite the One Sec timer, etc) and making it easier to block apps. I’m very happy with One Sec and would recommend it to anyone looking to make a change for the better.

One Sec not only forces you to take a moment to make sure that you truly should be using the app, but with the free re-intervention feature, it's far more effective than Apple's own Screen Time.

The app didn’t even recognize that it had blocked the website. Simply refreshing the website let me back in. After that, the blocking didn’t work at all, for that or for any website that I had put on my block list. What on earth is the point of a blocking app that doesn’t actually block anything?

Thank god I canceled before my free trial was up. It would have been a huge waste of my money on a useless app that does nothing when it comes to one of its most advertised features. Honestly, if I only intended to add one additional user to the subscription, what incentive is there in not receiving a discount? Look at it this way: 2x individual plans = $40; 2x users on family plan = $40. What's the difference? This is really shortsighted and selfish of the developer, in my opinion, and it makes me want to not even renew the individual subscription. $40 is too much. The app is good and well thought out, but it isn't actually providing that grand of a solution to justify that price, even for multiple users. $25 actually motivated me to add users to the app, given it was only a $5 increase from what I was paying. Doubling the price only frustrates me and makes me want to protest the developer's greed, and it shows that their intent isn't to actually provide a solution and make that accessible to more people, but to squeeze every dollar from their user base. What a careless decision towards users. I'll be deleting the app.

title: Brilliant
body:

I’m someone who uses various ways to make my devices more “dumb” or minimal. I mix this with feed blockers, screen time settings, greyscale, and not having social media apps on my phone. This is a very important piece of my already pretty elaborate puzzle.

This app can probably do more than I can grasp right now. I just use it to slow load apps and make them get progressively slower overtime. As my dopamine rush gets slower every time I wait for an app to load, I could just delete this app out of frustration. But I don’t. I feel like a kid knowing maybe it’s best if only mom can open the cookie jar. I also use the app for app blocking which is super cool. 

My only request is if I could set a timer for app blocking. What I mean: set timer and in 25 minutes all apps on the list will be blocked. That way maybe when I need or want to go down the rabbit hole, there is going to be a hard cutoff upcoming that I can’t stop. Otherwise I’ll just willingly not stop and go down a binge, which I unfortunately too often do.

title: Lifesaver of a time-saver
body:
I’ve been trying a few things to make my phone more annoying to use, or helpful when I do, and not a boredom eraser. One Sec is something that I wish I had years ago. I finally feel like I have the opportunity to fill my downtime with something other than my phone screen! By the way, I’m not sure why people are complaining about the price. $20 for a whole year is practically nothing.

Something I’d like to be able to do with the app is set a time limit on how long you can use a particular app before the interventions start. That way (if I’m good) I don’t have to wait for the intervention while I’m out at the store and trying to look something up before buying it, for example.

The other app is called ScreenZen and the purpose was identical to One Sec. How they achieved the wait period before the app was opened was utilizing the app restrictions function. More importantly what I think One Sec can learn from ScreenZen is implementing a timer on the app. So ScreenZen had an option where once the app was unlocked it would be automatically be locked or restricted after X amount of time. The user than had to go through the waiting period again. I think One Sec could really thrive with that feature because the 15 minute notification is nice but not damning enough. I wouldn’t be surprised if majority of people (including me) just ignore that. When I used ScreenZen after the app time limit was up many times I didn’t want to wait so I got productive. It’s a feature I think is very useful.

I also want to add ScreenZen’s method of using the app restriction settings makes blocking apps easier. So for OneSec you have to make a shortcut for each and every app. ScreenZen you just choose from a menu and the app is restricted. It’s much more convenient!

I really hope this feedback helps and I appreciate your app being an app blocker and an adult content blocker with a settings lock. It has really helped me in my personal life.

The dev has gone above and beyond to provide tutorials that are easy to access and follow, but it’s a significant time investment to get everything going.

That said, that time is well worth the investment and your actual change in app habits will return what you put in and way more.

Finally, I would pay double or triple the cost given what this app does for me. It’s hard to quantify the value of the increased focus and presence I’ve already noticed with my partner and children.

Download it now, put the time in to set it up, and don’t look back. :)

title: No Words Can Describe This One
body:
I have so many feelings and emotions to express but I’ll keep it brief. I don’t ever review apps, but I just had to with this one. For some, it has become a life-destroying experience, taking away time, decreasing productivity, increasing the risk of depression and more. It’s also impossible to simply delete and remove completely because of how embedded they are in our lives.

That’s where this app comes in, to curb our impulsive behaviors that make us doom scroll to no end. Days upon days I’ve lost before I had this app, and I wish I was joking. Although extraordinarily simple, the intervention feature of this app has instantly shown me how often I truly use these apps. 
There have been times where I close the app due to intervention, and open it again just seconds later not realizing that I’m being stopped multiple times. 
Has my memory deteriorated this much? It’s eye opening. The sheer level of benefit this app has is beyond anything I’ve experienced before, and I’d like to thank the developers for creating it. 

Thanks for bringing time back into my life, I can finally enjoy doing other things instead of mindlessly scrolling away like a zombie. What a world we live in. 

GET THIS APP NOW! I also hope Apple makes intervention a default feature at some point.

title: It’s okay
body:
This app, while limited in its free version, has helped me realize how much I use Instagram and led me to stop using it as much. However, there are some QoL things that are very annoying that drive my number up yet seem to only be fixable through the premium “intentional app switching” feature:

• Answering a text - if a text appears as a notification and you swipe down to respond, the app reads this as you leaving the app and restarts one sec
• Taking a screenshot - if you take a screenshot and tap it to crop / edit it, the app reads this as opening the photos app and makes you restart the one sec process after saving the screenshot.
• Swiping up (task manager) - when you swipe up slightly on an iPhone to view the task manager, it shows a scrolling field of apps. If I am copying information from one app to the next, however, it reads me entering task manager as closing the app and requires a restart. 
• Changing profile picture (Instagram) - I haven’t been able to replicate this, but when I was changing my Instagram profile picture, my photo albums opened to show me choices. One sec read this (only this one time) as opening Photos and restarted one sec when I was done

title: Another Subscription Based App that Offers Slim to Nothing
body:
Want an app that actually wants to help you reduce screen time? This one isnt it. They just want your money. 

Another greedy app that requires a SUBSCRIPTION to use. Which is $15 a year. Please, people, take into consideration of what a $15 app should do for you, this one runs a very very simple program when you open an app, its worth should be free with minimal ads, and maybe 99 cents without adds (permanently, not months payment). You people need to stop supporting greedy applications like this, know your worth, and know what apps are worth. The only things that should be subscription based are TV and Media, apps like this should and used to be around $1-$4 in total, not a monthly payment. 

So why does it seem like every app these days require a subscription? Because people fall for it and some even forget that they are subscribed to it when they sign up for a free trial, so the app devs can get away with it and be well off with it despite the fact that more people would use these apps if they poored more love and passion into their apps. It also doesn't help that Apple themselves have fairly high prices for devs to keep apps on the app store, greed promotes greed. I, along with most sensible human beings, will never buy something subscription based unless it is related to TV or other forms Media. When you buy a simple application, your supposed to own it indefinitely, there should be a lot of settings to optimize it to your needs, thats what should be and used to be in apps, sometimes even free ones. But now your practically renting an app for quadruple the price that its worth and its not even equipped with settings or the ability to optimize the app to your needs. So what should you do? Well I would say your best bet would be to buy an Android phone and use apps off the Google Play store, as finding quality apps with reasonable prices on the App Store is near impossible, on the Google Play store it is less impossible, but still rare to find. Plus you can directly download applications from the web, though you have to make sure its a reliable source.

Dont get me wrong, I love the idea this app offers as I wouldn't have downloaded it if I didn't. But the price for such a simple program that I'm sure 1 guy made in less than 2 months is absolutely ridiculous, and the fact its subscription based instantly proves that they are not on your side. Think of it this way, this is the type of app you would like to have for at least a few months if not years, so the cost just keeps adding up, when its really worth maybe 1-2 dollars.

title: Thank you
body:
So few developers are investing in practical solutions for the problems created by social media, so I really appreciate this app's existence!

The app does about as good a job as the iOS platform will allow it to. There are some minor annoyances with how Shortcuts work (can't hide "Running your automation" notifications, can't duplicate / templatize automations, etc.) but I can't fault the author for any of this.

Some gripes that are within the author's control:

• I don't want a count of how many times I've tried to open the app. A huge part of my motivation for cutting down on social media is reducing the influence of numbers (likes, shares, metrics) on my behavior. And sure, this number is better aligned with my personal goals than any of the numbers Twitter shoves in my face, but if I could turn it off, I would.

• Please stop asking me to rate your app every time I choose the "don't open" option. Once is enough! This is the reason I docked a star.

title: Meh
body:
First I got to say I am using the free version. It gives you one app to use the function for. Which is fine and I do not criticize. 

However, my two star review is mainly made up of for one it more often than not asks you to upgrade to pro instead of giving you the one deep breath exercise which makes me more annoyed than helps me to be more mindful. 

I didn’t know I could only have one app which is why I had a second app set up with it. The app then prompted me to either upgrade to pro or chose between the two apps. I chose and even deleted the action I said up in shortcuts but it will ask me now to choose between both apps or upgrade over and over again. Pretty annoying bug. 

And then, money might not be a factor for you, but it is for me, so this last point might be irrelevant; I do not understand what justifies the price of the app for the full version. $50 for a perpetual license is just not realistic for the average person, neither adding yet another subscription of $4 per month ($18.5 if you pay for the whole year up front). I really wish app creators would realize this. 

TL;DR I like the idea but it’s too buggy in general and too spammy with their subscription service which is also overpriced. I will just uninstall and go back to leaving my phone in a different room again.
